en: Thus have I heard— Majjhima Nikāya 104, the Sāmagāma Sutta.
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling among the Sakyans at Sāmagāma.
Now at that time, Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta had recently passed away at Pāvā.
Following his death, the Nigaṇṭhas were split and divided, falling into factions, engaged in quarrels and disputes, and living while piercing one another with verbal weapons:
“You do not understand this Dhamma and Discipline; I understand this Dhamma and Discipline.
How could you understand this Dhamma and Discipline? You have practiced wrongly; I have practiced rightly. My [position] is consistent; yours is inconsistent.
What should have been said first, you said last; what should have been said last, you said first. You have overstepped [the bounds].”
"You have been refuted. Your position has been overturned. You are defeated; go forth to seek release from your argument, or provide an explanation if you are able.
Indeed, it seems as though there is only slaughter among the Nigaṇṭhas, followers of Nātaputta.
Even those lay disciples of the Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta who wear white robes [behave] likewise toward the Nigaṇṭhas, followers of Nātaputta.
Disgusted with form, detached from form, and turned away from form— just as one would be toward a poorly proclaimed and poorly expounded Dhamma and Vinaya that is not conducive to liberation,
not conducive to peace, not proclaimed by a Perfectly Enlightened One, where the stupa is broken and there is no refuge—
then the novice Cunda, having completed the rains retreat at Pāvā, approached the Venerable Ānanda at Sāmagāma.
Having approached and paid homage to the Venerable Ānanda, he sat down to one side.
Sitting there, the novice Cunda said this to the Venerable Ānanda:
"Venerable sir, the Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta has recently passed away in Pāvā."
“With his passing away, the Nigaṇṭhas have split and become divided... [as above] ...with their monuments shattered and left without a refuge.
When this was said, the Venerable Ānanda said to the novice Cunda:
“Friend Cunda, this is a subject for discussion that merits an audience with the Blessed One.”
"Come, friend Cunda, let us approach the Blessed One; having approached, we shall report this matter to the Blessed One.
"Very well, venerable sir," the novice Cunda replied to the Venerable Ānanda.
Then the Venerable Ānanda and the novice Cunda went to where the Blessed One was; having approached, they...
Having paid homage to the Blessed One, they sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, the Venerable Ānanda said this to the Blessed One:
"Venerable sir, this novice monk Cunda spoke thus:"
“Venerable sir, the Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta has recently passed away at Pāvā.
With his passing, the Nigaṇṭhas have split and become divided... [as before] ...with their monuments shattered and without a refuge.
Venerable sir, this thought occurred to me:
“Let there be no dispute in the Saṅgha after the passing away of the Blessed One;
for such a dispute would be for the harm of many, for the unhappiness of many, for the ruin, harm, and suffering of many, including gods and humans.
“What do you think, Ānanda?”
"Ānanda, do you see these things that have been taught by me through direct knowledge—
the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases for psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers,
the seven factors of enlightenment, and the noble eightfold path?"
"Are there even two bhikkhus who hold different views? "Venerable sir, regarding those things taught by the Blessed One through direct knowledge—

namely, the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases for psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the noble eightfold path— I do not see even two bhikkhus among these teachings who hold different views."
“But, Bhante, those individuals who dwell as if seeking refuge with the Blessed One might, after the Blessed One’s passing, create a dispute in the Saṅgha regarding livelihood or the Pātimokkha.
That dispute would be for the harm of many, for the unhappiness of many, for the ruin, harm, and suffering of many, including devas and humans.
“Ānanda, that dispute—namely, regarding livelihood or the Pātimokkha—is a very minor matter.”

For, Ānanda, if a dispute concerning the path or the way of practice were to arise in the Saṅgha, that dispute would lead to the harm of many people, to the suffering of many people, to the detriment, harm, and misery of many people, including both gods and humans.
Ānanda, there are these six roots of dispute.
What are the six?
In this case, Ānanda, a bhikkhu is prone to anger and harbors resentment.
Such a bhikkhu, Ānanda, dwells disrespectful and undeferential toward the Teacher,
dwells disrespectful and undeferential toward the Dhamma, dwells disrespectful and undeferential toward the Saṅgha, and [toward] the training as well.
He does not fulfill [the training].

Ānanda, that bhikkhu who dwells disrespectful and undeferential toward the Teacher, who dwells disrespectful and undeferential toward the Dhamma, and who dwells disrespectful and undeferential toward the Saṅgha, does not fulfill the training;
he gives rise to dispute within the Saṅgha. He who is...
Dispute is for the harm of many people, for the unhappiness of many people, for the detriment, harm, and suffering of many people, including both gods and humans.
If you, Ānanda, should perceive such a root of dispute within yourselves or externally, then, Ānanda, you should strive for the abandoning of that very evil root of dispute.

If you do not perceive such a root of dispute, Ānanda, either within yourself or externally, then, Ānanda, you should practice for the sake of preventing the future outflow of that very same evil root of dispute.
In this way, there is the abandoning of that evil root of dispute; in this way, there is the prevention of the future outflow of that evil root of dispute.
Furthermore, Ānanda, a bhikkhu is one who slanders and is prone to resentment... [and so forth].
He is envious and stingy … he is fraudulent and deceitful … he has evil desires and wrong view … [and so on].
He is one who clings to his own views, is obstinate in grasping them, and is difficult to disabuse of them.
Ānanda, that monk who clings to his own views, is obstinate in grasping them, and is difficult to disabuse of them, dwells without respect and without deference toward the Teacher;
he dwells without respect and without deference toward the Dhamma; he dwells without respect [toward the Saṅgha].
He dwells without deference and does not fulfill the training.

Ānanda, that bhikkhu who dwells without respect and deference toward the Teacher, and who does not fulfill the training in the Dhamma, the Saṅgha, and the training, creates a dispute within the Saṅgha;
and whatever dispute there is, it is for the harm of many people, for the unhappiness of many people.
This leads to the harm, disadvantage, and suffering of many people, including both gods and humans.
Ānanda, if you perceive such a root of dispute within yourselves or among others, you should strive, Ānanda, to abandon that very evil root of dispute.
If you do not perceive such a root of dispute within yourselves or among others, then, Ānanda, you should practice so that that very evil root of dispute does not arise in the future.
In this way, there is the abandoning of this evil root of dispute; in this way, there is the future non-recurrence of this evil root of dispute.
These, Ānanda, are the six roots of dispute.
There are, Ānanda, these four legal issues.
Which four?
The legal issue arising from disputes, the legal issue arising from accusations, the legal issue arising from offenses, and the legal issue arising from business—
these, Ānanda, are the four legal issues.

Moreover, Ānanda, there are these seven principles for settling legal issues—for the settling and pacification of legal issues as they arise: the resolution face-to-face should be granted; the resolution through recollection should be granted;

the resolution because of past insanity should be granted; it should be dealt with according to what has been admitted; the majority decision; the further penalty; and the covering over as with grass.
And how, Ānanda, is there a resolution face-to-face?
Here, Ānanda, monks dispute, saying either "this is Dhamma" or "this is not Dhamma," or "this is Vinaya" or "this is not Vinaya.
In such a case, Ānanda, all those monks must assemble together in harmony.
Having assembled, the guide of the Dhamma should be reviewed.
Having reviewed the guide of the Dhamma, that legal issue should be settled in such a way that it accords with it.
In this way, Ānanda, there is a resolution face-to-face.
And thus, Ānanda, there is the settling of certain legal issues here, namely, by means of resolution in the presence of the parties (*sammukhāvinaya*).
And how, Ānanda, does a decision by a majority (*yebhuyyasikā*) come about?
If those monks, Ānanda, are not able to settle that legal dispute in that monastery,
then those monks, Ānanda, should go to whichever monastery has a larger number of monks.
There, everyone must assemble in harmony.
Having assembled, the guide of the Dhamma should be reviewed.
Having reviewed the guide of the Dhamma, that legal issue should be settled in such a way that it accords with it.
This, Ānanda, is the majority decision; and in this way there comes to be the settling of certain legal issues here, namely—
By means of a majority decision.
And how, Ānanda, does the verdict of mindfulness occur?
Here, Ānanda, monks reprove a monk for such a grave offense, either a *pārājika* or one bordering on a *pārājika*:
‘Venerable sir, do you remember having committed such a grave offense, one that is a pārājika or bordering on a pārājika?
He replies:
‘No indeed, friends, I do not remember having committed such a grave offense, one that is a pārājika or bordering on a pārājika.’
In that case, Ānanda, a verdict of mindfulness should be granted to that bhikkhu.
This, Ānanda, is how a verdict of mindfulness comes about; and in this way, certain legal issues are settled here, namely, by means of a verdict of mindfulness.
And how, Ānanda, is there a verdict of past insanity?
Here, Ānanda, monks reprove a monk for such a grave offense—either a *pārājika* or one bordering on a *pārājika*—saying:
"Does the venerable one remember having committed such a grave offense, a *pārājika* or one bordering on a *pārājika*?"
He speaks thus:
"Friends, I do not recall having committed such a grave offense, whether a pārājika or one bordering on a pārājika.
But he further entangles him as he attempts to extricate himself:
“Come now, venerable friend, find out properly whether you remember having committed such a grave offense—either a *pārājika* or one bordering on a *pārājika*.
He replied:
“Friend, I did indeed fall into madness, a derangement of the mind.”
"By that madman of mine, much that is unbefitting a recluse was practiced and spoken;
I do not remember it.
This was done by me while I was deluded."
In that case, Ānanda, the verdict of past insanity should be granted to that bhikkhu.
This, Ānanda, is how the verdict of past insanity comes about; and in this way, there is the settling of certain legal issues here, namely, by means of the verdict of past insanity.
And how, Ānanda, is there a formal act based on confession?
Here, Ānanda, a bhikkhu—whether accused or unaccused—remembers an offense, discloses it, and makes it plain.
That bhikkhu, Ānanda, should approach a senior bhikkhu, arrange his robe over one shoulder, pay homage at his feet, sit down in the kneeling position, raise his joined palms, and say this:
‘Venerable sir, I have fallen into such-and-such an offense; I confess it.
He says to him:
‘Do you see it?’
“Yes, I see it.
“You should exercise restraint in the future.
“I shall exercise restraint.”

In this way, Ānanda, there is the act of acting according to what has been admitted; and thus, in this world, there is the settlement of certain legal issues, namely, by means of acting according to what has been admitted.
And how, Ānanda, is there the procedure of further penalty?
In this case, Ānanda, a bhikkhu reproves another bhikkhu for such a grave offense—either a *pārājika* or one bordering on a *pārājika*—saying:
"Does the venerable one remember having committed such a grave offense, a *pārājika* or one bordering on a *pārājika*?
He replies thus:
“I do not recall, friend, having committed such a grave offense, whether a *pārājika* or one bordering on a *pārājika*.
But he, while attempting to evade it, presses him further:
“Come now, venerable sir, you should know this well: do you recall having committed such a grave offense, whether a *pārājika* or one bordering on a *pārājika*?”
He speaks thus:
“Friends, I do not recall having committed such a grave offense as a *pārājika* or one bordering on a *pārājika*;
however, friends, I do recall having committed such a minor offense.”
As he tried to extricate himself, the other entangled him even more, saying:
“Come now, Venerable, find out properly whether you remember having committed such a grave offense, one involving defeat or bordering on defeat.
He replied as follows:
"Friends, if I will acknowledge even such a minor offense as this when asked,
why then would I not acknowledge such a grave offense as a *pārājika* or one bordering on a *pārājika* when asked?
He spoke thus.
“Friend, having committed such a minor offense, you would not acknowledge it when questioned;
how then, having committed such a grave offense— either a *pārājika* or one bordering on a *pārājika*—
would you acknowledge it when questioned?”
“Come now, venerable friend, find out properly whether you remember having committed such a grave offense, one that is a *pārājika* or bordering on a *pārājika*.
He says this:
“I do indeed remember, friends, having committed such a grave offense, one that is a *pārājika* or bordering on a *pārājika*.”
‘This was said by me in jest;
this was said by me in play—I do not recall having committed such a grave offense, whether a pārājika or one bordering on a pārājika.
In this way, Ānanda, there is a verdict of ‘the worse offender,’ and in this way there is a settlement of certain legal issues, namely: [this verdict of the worse offender].”
Regarding the procedure for declaring one's own greater fault:
And how, Ānanda, does the "covering over with grass" take place?
Here, Ānanda, when monks who have fallen into quarreling, strife, and disputes dwell having practiced much that is unbecoming of a recluse and have uttered such things repeatedly.
Then, Ānanda, all the bhikkhus must assemble in harmony.

Having assembled, a competent bhikkhu from among those on one side should rise from his seat, arrange his robe over one shoulder, and, having extended his hands in reverential salutation, inform the Saṅgha:
"Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha hear me."
While we were living in mutual strife, quarreling, and engaged in disputes, much that was unbecoming of a recluse was practiced and uttered by us.

If it seems appropriate to the Saṅgha, for the sake of these venerable ones and for my own sake, I shall [confess] in the midst of the Saṅgha by means of the "covering over with grass" (tiṇavatthāraka) regarding whatever offense has been committed by these venerable ones and whatever offense has been committed by myself.
‘...I would speak, setting aside grave offenses and setting aside matters connected with householders.
Then, a competent monk from among those monks who side together should rise from his seat, arrange his robe over one shoulder, raise his joined palms in salutation, and inform the Saṅgha:
‘Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha hear me. ...’”
While we were living in quarreling, disputing, and contending, we have committed much that is unbecoming of a recluse,
both spoken and practiced. If it seems appropriate to the Saṅgha, for the sake of these venerable ones and for my own sake,
I shall [confess] in the midst of the Saṅgha by means of the "covering over as with grass" (tiṇavatthāraka).
‘I would speak, setting aside grave offenses and setting aside matters connected with householders.
It is in this way, Ānanda, that there is the ‘covering over as with grass,’ and it is by means of this covering over as with grass that some legal issues are settled here.
"Ānanda, these six qualities are endearing, inspiring affection, inspiring respect, leading to inclusion, non-dispute, harmony, and unity.
What are the six?
Here, Ānanda, a bhikkhu maintains bodily conduct imbued with loving-kindness toward his fellow celibates, both openly and in private."
This quality, too, is memorable, endearing, and inspiring; it leads to inclusion, to non-dispute, to harmony, and to unity.
Furthermore, Ānanda, a bhikkhu maintains loving verbal conduct toward his fellow practitioners both openly and in private.
This quality, too, is memorable, endearing, and inspiring; it leads to inclusion, to non-dispute, to harmony, and to unity.
Furthermore, Ānanda, a bhikkhu maintains a mind of loving-kindness toward his fellow practitioners, both openly and in private.
This quality is memorable, endearing, and inspiring; it leads to being gathered together, to absence of dispute, to harmony, and to unity.
Furthermore, Ānanda, whatever gains are righteous and righteously obtained—even if only the mere contents of an alms bowl—[he shares them with his fellow practitioners...]
With such gains, he is one who shares his possessions without making distinctions, sharing them in common with virtuous companions in the holy life.
This quality is consoling, it creates affection, it creates respect, and it leads to inclusion, to lack of dispute, to harmony, and to unity.
Furthermore, Ānanda, a bhikkhu possesses those virtues that are unbroken, untorn, unblemished, and stainless...
Regarding such virtues that are unshackled, praised by the wise, unadhered-to, and conducive to concentration—
one dwells having attained a commonality of virtue with one’s fellow celibates, both openly and in private. This quality, too, is memorable,
creates affection, inspires respect, and leads to gathering together, to absence of dispute, to harmony, and to unity.

Furthermore, Ānanda, a bhikkhu dwells both in public and in private possessing in common with his companions in the holy life that view which is noble, emancipating, and leads the one who practices it to the complete destruction of suffering.
This, too, is a principle of cordiality that creates affection, creates respect, and leads to gathering together, to non-dispute, to harmony, and to unity.
These, Ānanda, are the six principles of cordiality that create affection and respect, and lead to gathering together, to non-dispute, to harmony, and to unity.
“If you, Ānanda, were to undertake and practice these six principles of cordiality, do you see, Ānanda, any course of speech—whether subtle or gross—that you would not tolerate?
“Certainly not, Bhante.
“Therefore, Ānanda, undertake and practice these six principles of cordiality.”
"That will lead to your welfare and happiness for a long time.
Thus spoke the Blessed One.
The Venerable Ānanda, being uplifted, rejoiced in the words of the Blessed One.
The Sāmagāma Sutta, the fourth, is finished.
